RT @BitcoinNewsCom: LEDGER HARDWARE WALLET IMPLANTS WERE DISCOVERED OVER A YEAR BEFORE THIS WEEK’S SUPPLY-CHAIN ATTACK REVELATIONS

Renowned hardware security researcher and computer engineer Joe Grand (@joegrand), also known as “Kingpin,” explains how he was contacted in August 2025 by a man in Thailand who had discovered a compromised Ledger Nano X.

The man had purchased a cheap Ledger online to replace the battery in his existing device. 

When he opened it, he discovered a smaller battery, unauthorized circuitry, additional wiring, and an antenna.

After posting his discovery on Reddit and reportedly receiving little interest from local police, he contacted Grand to investigate.

The discovery came more than a year before the Ledger supply-chain attack became a major public controversy, with nearly $100 million in cryptocurrency reportedly stolen this week.

items.content:
RT @oegerikus: For the second time in Google Chrome’s history, Google awarded a $250,000 bounty for a full-chain exploit… to @XBOW. Here’s the full story:

At an all-hands at the start of 2026 in Malta, I set the team a crazy challenge. A full-chain exploit of Chrome by the annual Black Hat cybersecurity conference in August.

I believed there were few better tests of whether @XBOW could move beyond web applications to desktop software, servers and devices.

Chrome is one of the most hardened pieces of software on the planet, used by more than half the world’s population.

A full-chain exploit lets an attacker take total control of a machine, where they can read every email, password and bank login the user types. You don’t need to download anything or click a phishing link. Visiting the wrong site is enough.

So @moyix, Andres Luksenberg, Baul Lee, and Willem Pinckaers took on the challenge along with a fifth teammate: OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol. 

They built a chain they thought would win, but Google told us they already knew one of the bugs. 

We were already in Las Vegas for Black Hat and DEF CON, and the team didn’t want to go home without the win.

So Brendan and the agents built a new exploit in just 6 days. 

We submitted it to Google and waited.

The news came through that we'd done what should’ve been impossible. A full-chain bounty of $250,000, the first awarded under Google’s 2026 rules.

It took just 6 days and $40,000 of compute to construct an exploit that affects a billion users of Chrome on Windows. An intelligence-agency veteran told me his team used to spend 6 months on this kind of vulnerability.

My takeaway: the cost of finding truly critical vulnerabilities is collapsing, for attackers and defenders alike. Restricting powerful models is not the answer; GPT-5.6 Sol is already public.

But defenders have one advantage attackers never will: they can test their own code first. 

Assume your software is exploitable. Whoever is hunting your bugs has the same building blocks we did.

This is cause for urgency but not panic.

XBOW is now developing an autonomous product for testing compiled software (desktop applications, servers, embedded devices), and partnering with the world’s top organizations to design that product. 

If you’d like to be one of them, get in touch. 

P.S. Restart Chrome whenever the Update button appears!

items.content:
RT @PalmerLuckey: I am getting lots of incoming questions about the public execution of Nidal Hasan, mostly because I have been outspoken on wanting public executions for over a decade.

My position is simple:  Executions should be public and brutal, not private and medicalized.  They are the ultimate example of the state's monopoly on violence, and the only way to keep that from running out of control is to confront voters with the trade they have made every single time, that they might have appropiate confidence or revulsion in the institution.

This is not new thinking.  George Washington thought the same.  The way we have shifted from hanging to firing squads to doctors quietly injecting chemicals that send our worst gently off to sleep is awful and dystopian, a total short-circuiting of important feedback mechanisms.  It makes needless executions more likely, not less so.  People who demean this as barbaric or yucky miss the whole point.  It doesn't somehow become torture or inhumane (as the UN is suddenly claiming) just because we decline to hide the act behind a curtain.

And then there are those who suggest any revel in the death of those who truly deserve it is an indicator of a broken or diseased mind.  To the contrary.  It is normal, good, and aligned with our natural and national order.  That it has not been done here in 60 years is an indictment in and of itself.

And that is without even getting into the fact that men were not hung for stealing horse, but that horses may not be stolen.

"I would to God that one of the most attrocious in each State was hung in Gibbets, up on a gallows five times as high as the one prepared by Haman. No punishment, in my opinion, is too great for the Man, who can build his greatness upon his Country’s ruin." 
- George Washington, 1778

items.content:
RT @poteto: i love writing. i never let agents write for me. whether it's docs, or tweets, or shitposts, or even prompts (okay maybe that one's harder as agents manage other agents) 

there's a simple reason for that: i still strongly believe that writing is thinking. it's a skill i hope to never give up. it's also important to me that whatever i say is always authentic, mistakes and all. my favorite posts are the ones that i just full send without any editing

i suspect it also helps with prompting. being able to clearly express what i want, and knowing the vocabulary i need to be able to direct my agents does seem to make for more effective usage of agents. in the same way that engineers have an advantage when we prompt agents to write code, because we are intimately familiar with the words that make up the discipline

knowing the right word incantations to get an agent to produce a desired goal almost feels like spellcasting. as models get more capable, and that input box looks more and more like a magic box that can output anything, words become the interface between you and the genie

there may come a time when we give up the keyboard in exchange for brain-computer interfaces. but until then, i'm writing every word.

items.content:
The owner bought the car used and asked for a basic cybersecurity check.

Nothing was wrong with the car mechanically. No warning lights, no battery drain, no strange behaviour.

But while going through the infotainment and telematics settings, I noticed something that would bother me if it were my own car.

The previous owner’s profile was still present.

That alone is not unusual.

People trade in cars every day without properly resetting the infotainment system.

What made this one more interesting was that the telematics module was still making outbound connections shortly after the ignition came on.

So I started looking at the traffic from the vehicle’s connected-services side.

The car was reaching cloud endpoints normally used for things like remote services, vehicle status, app syncing, and account-based features.

Again, that does not mean anything malicious was happening.

The real question was simpler:

Whose account was the car still associated with?

I checked the local infotainment profiles, paired phones, and connected-service settings.

There it was.

The previous owner’s account had never been removed.

That means the physical car had changed hands, but part of its digital identity had not.

Depending on the manufacturer and which services are enabled, connected-car accounts can be tied to things like vehicle location, remote lock status, maintenance data, trip information, charging information, or app-based controls.

Not every platform exposes the same features, but the principle is the same.

Ownership of the car and ownership of the digital account should match.

I documented the existing profile, removed the stale pairing, factory-reset the infotainment data, and verified that the telematics account was properly transferred.

After the reset, the old profile was gone and the expected onboarding process appeared instead.

This is one of those things people rarely think about when buying or selling a car.

They clear the glovebox.

They remove the toll tag.

They take out the garage remote.

But they forget that the car may also contain account data, paired phones, contact history, navigation destinations, Wi-Fi profiles, and cloud-linked services.

A used car should not only be mechanically inspected.

It should be digitally cleaned too.

Because sometimes the previous owner leaves more behind than a receipt in the centre console.
